summary: This experimental memo describes how 1993 ISO X.500 protocols can be used to manage the root naming context of the directory. The settings it uses are supplementary to the X.500 standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Every phone book needs a first page that says where the other books are, and this explains how to look after that page.

questions: what is the x.500 fast track solution
how is the x.500 root shadowed to other servers
subtitle: Using X.500 standard protocols to manage the root of the directory tree

tldr.problem: X.500 directories need a root entry, but the standard says the root is managed through bilateral agreements between all top-level directory servers, which becomes unmanageable as more servers are added.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2120 proposes three solutions of increasing complexity to use standard X.500 replication and operational binding protocols to manage the root context through a central root server, rather than requiring every top-level server to coordinate directly with all others.
tldr.outcome: This was experimental because the X.500 standard had defects that required corrections. The solutions ranged from a fast track (knowledge distribution) to longer-term approaches requiring standard amendments.

today: RFC 2120 is Experimental. X.500 never achieved the widespread adoption on the Internet that was envisioned, so these solutions remained proposals. LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, RFC 3377) became the dominant standard for directory services instead.

sections.title: The X.500 Root Context Problem
sections.content:
X.500 is an international directory protocol for looking up information about people, organizations and services. At the top of the directory tree is the root context, which holds information about first-level entries (like countries or top-level organizations).

The X.500 standard says first-level directory servers should manage the root context through bilateral agreements with each other. But as the number of servers grows, this becomes impractical: each new server must negotiate with all existing ones, and managing the root becomes chaotic.
sections.plainLanguage: A big library has a main desk that tells you where books on each topic are. Someone has to update that main desk every time a new section is added.

sections.title: Moving from Proprietary to Standard Solutions
sections.content:
The NameFLOW-Paradise X.500 service had solved this problem with a proprietary approach: a single central root server (called Giant Tortoise) held all country entries and replicated them to every other server. This worked well but was not standard.

RFC 2120 describes the plan to migrate to solutions that use standard X.500 protocols (DISP for replication, DOP for operational bindings) without losing the performance benefits of the centralized approach. The proposal includes three tracks with increasing capability and complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: They had a private solution that worked well, but now they want to switch to the official rulebook while keeping it working just as well.

sections.title: The Fast Track: Knowledge Distribution
sections.content:
The fast track solution uses only the Directory Information Shadowing Protocol (DISP) and minimal changes to the X.500 standard. Each top-level server shadows (copies) the root context from the central root server. This approach distributes knowledge about where each country's server is located, and allows insecure List operations (searching the root).

It does not include access control information in the copied root context, so List operations at the root are not protected. However, first-level entries like countries are usually public anyway. The fast track was expected to be available in DSA products by the end of 1996.
sections.plainLanguage: Each server gets a copy of the root directory from the main server. You can look up what is where, but everyone can see it.

sections.title: Slower and Long-Term Solutions
sections.content:
The slower track adds support for fully secure one-level Search operations at the root by distributing access control information. It requires corrections to the X.500 standard itself, which are proposed as defect reports (included in annexes of the RFC).

The long-term solution (not expected until 1998 or later) uses hierarchical operational bindings (HOBs) managed by the Directory Operational Protocol (DOP) instead of DISP. This is the cleanest solution from a standard perspective but requires more extensive protocol support in DSA implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The medium-term solution lets you search securely. The long-term solution uses the most official method, but not many systems support it yet.

sections.title: Standards Defects and Proposed Corrections
sections.content:
RFC 2120 identifies defects in the 1993 X.500 standard that prevent the solutions from working as intended. For example, the standard does not specify how to include access control information in shadowed root context, or how to handle one-level Search in a shadowed copy of the root.

The RFC includes defect report texts proposed to ISO (the standards body). These amendments are necessary for the slower and long-term solutions to work properly. The annex also notes the restriction in the 1993 standard that limits which attributes can be passed in certain operations.
sections.plainLanguage: The official rulebook has some missing instructions, and this RFC proposes what should be added to make the new system work correctly.

references.text: Kille, S., "Replication and Distributed Operations extensions to provide an Internet Directory using X.500", UCL, November 1991.
